title: The oxygen dissociation curve and the Bohr shift
caption: In the lungs haemoglobin is almost fully saturated. In respiring tissue, where pO₂ is low, the steep middle of the curve means a small fall in pO₂ releases a lot of oxygen. More CO₂ shifts the curve right (lower affinity), so even more is released; fetal haemoglobin's curve lies to the left (higher affinity).
alt: S-shaped oxygen dissociation curves of percentage saturation against partial pressure of oxygen, with the curve for high carbon dioxide shifted right and fetal haemoglobin shifted left.
description: The horizontal axis is the partial pressure of oxygen in kilopascals, from 0 to 14. The vertical axis is percentage saturation of haemoglobin, from 0 to 100.
The adult curve is S-shaped (sigmoid): flat at low partial pressure, steep in the middle, and levelling off near 97% at the partial pressure in the lungs (about 13 kPa).

The curve at high carbon dioxide (the Bohr effect) lies to the right of it: at the same partial pressure, haemoglobin is less saturated, so it has given up more oxygen. An arrow at 4 kPa shows the extra oxygen unloaded.
The fetal haemoglobin curve lies to the left: at the same partial pressure it is more saturated, so it can take oxygen from the mother's blood.
Shaded bands mark the partial pressures typical of respiring tissue and of the lungs. Curves drawn from the Hill equation with textbook values; real values vary.
